629	                             4. Discussion
630	                                   The main aim of this study was to determine whether professional soccer players
631	                             who contracted SARS-CoV-2 had an increased risk of muscular injuries. The find-
632	                             ings of this study reported a three to five times increased risk of muscle injury after
633	                             SARS-CoV-2 infection.
634	                                   Over the years, UEFA has conducted numerous studies on the match/minute ratio
635	                             played by the elite athletes of the teams participating in its international tournaments
636	                             to define a “normal” value for the incidence of injuries in football [22–24]. In particular,
637	                             Hägglund et al.’s 11-year retrospective study [23] observed the incidence of injuries in more
638	                             than 1000 h of play and found an incidence of 2 injuries per year per individual footballer
639	                             or an average of 50 injuries if we take into consideration the team group (list of 25 athletes).
640	                             If we consider only muscular injuries, the incidence drops to 15 injuries out of a shortlist of
641	                             25 footballers, with an average per athlete of 0.6 injuries [22]. These data are essential for
642	                             commenting on the results of our study. Our results showed that in both leagues, players
643	                             who did not contract COVID-19 had injury rates lower than the average of 0.6 reported by
644	                             Bengtsson et al. [22] in both seasons. Instead, regarding players infected with SARS-CoV-2,
645	                             they showed in the pre-COVID season an injury rate in line with the data of Bengtsson
646	                             et al. [22], while in the 2020/2021 season, after the infection, it increased significantly in
647	 Infect. Dis. Rep. 2023, 15                                                                                              432
648	
649	
650	
651	
652	                             both leagues (1.44 for Serie A and 1.23 for LaLiga). The results relating to the change
653	                             between seasons within individual groups showed significant differences in both groups;
654	                             however, it should be specified that with such large samples, it is highly probable that even
655	                             minimal variations between seasons are significant (especially in the C− group which is
656	                             substantially larger than the C+ group), while if we look at the 95% confidence intervals
657	                             we see an higher increase in number of injuries in the 2020/2021 season among football
658	                             players who have had COVID-19.
659	                                   The results of minutes and matches played showed that in Serie A the players in the
660	                             C+ group, during the 2019/2020 season, played more games and in total more minutes
661	                             than the players in group C−; in the 2020/2021 season, the players in group C+ (which
662	                             contracted COVID-19 during this season), they played fewer games and in total fewer
663	                             minutes than in the previous season, on the contrary the players in group C− obtained
664	                             an increase in total games and minutes played. This could be caused both by the period
665	                             of absence linked to the infection itself and by the greater number of muscle injuries that
666	                             players in group C+ have suffered, forcing them to have a longer period of absence from
667	                             sporting activity. The same, albeit to a lesser extent, is observed in the Spanish league
668	                             showing a substantial overlap of minutes played and games played in the 19/20 season
669	                             between the two groups; however, in the following season, there was a reduction in minutes
670	                             and games played in group C+ and an increase in games played and a slight reduction
671	                             in minutes played in group C−. Our results indicate that SARS-CoV-2 infection could be
672	                             a risk factor for muscular injury, in line with the recent study by Wezenbeek et al. [15].
673	                             Multiple linear regression analysis showed that in the 2019–2020 season, the risk of injury
674	                             was significantly influenced by age, according to a previous study by Green et al. [25].
675	                             However, in the 2020–2021 season, SARS-CoV-2 infection was the variable that highly
676	                             influenced the risk of muscle injury. Therefore, belonging to the C+ group in the 2020–2021
677	                             season completely distorts the correlation between the various variables and the muscle
678	                             injury rates, becoming the main factor capable of influencing the latter. In other words,
679	                             while older players with a high number of games and playing time were at greater risk of
680	                             incurring muscle injuries in the 2019–2020 season, having contracted COVID-19 was the
681	                             primary and most important risk factor in the following season. Similarly, in LaLiga, age
682	                             was the main risk factor for muscle injury in the 2019–2020 season, while in the 2020–2021
683	                             season, the only variable that significantly influenced muscle injuries was the SARS-CoV-2
684	                             infection. The survival analysis showed that during the 2019–2020 season, the two groups
685	                             had a similar risk of muscular injury. In the 2020/2021 season, the hazard risk ratio was 3.7
686	                             to 5.1 times greater among those athletes infected by SARS-CoV-2, in line with the results
687	                             of Wezenbeek et al. [15], which reported a five-time higher hazard rate to develop a muscle
688	                             strain after SARS-CoV-2 infection. One of the reasons that could explain the age effect only
689	                             in the Italian league and not in the Spanish may depend on the fact that age is a variable
690	                             not always correlated to injury. In fact, a recent review [26] reported that age influences
691	                             athletes’ risk of calf muscle injuries, while another review [27] showed that age is not linked
692	                             to a higher risk of quadriceps muscle injury. Nevertheless, the source of our data is not
693	                             specific to the type of injury and therefore it was not possible to carry out a sub-analysis.
694	                             Future studies will have to consider this element to draw definitive conclusions regarding
695	                             the role of age on the risk of injuries.
696	                                   As discussed by Wezenbeek et al. [15], there are two possible explanations for the
697	                             correlation between SARS-CoV-2 infection and an increased risk of muscular injury. The
698	                             first hypothesis is that strict quarantine rules implemented during the 2020/2021 season
699	                             led to prolonged periods of abstention from training and sports participation, resulting in
700	                             muscular detraining [28,29] and subsequent loss of muscle strength [30]. Muscle strength
701	                             has been shown to be a protective factor against muscular injury [31], and the loss of muscle
702	                             strength is more significant in highly trained athletes with greater initial muscle mass [32].
703	                             The second explanation is related to the direct biological effects of the virus. SARS-CoV-2
704	                             infection causes hyperinflammation, an increase in inflammatory markers, an increase
705	                             in the neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio, and possible depletion of circulating T cells [33].
706	 Infect. Dis. Rep. 2023, 15                                                                                                      433
707	
708	
709	
710	
711	                             Furthermore, the virus may cause direct damage to muscle tissue by targeting the ACE 2
712	                             receptor [17], which is widely present in muscle tissue [34]. In addition, the virus can cause
713	                             disturbances in blood flow and oxygen transport, leading to reduced muscle oxygenation
714	                             during exercise. Lower muscle oxygen saturation [35] and VO2 max [36] are possible risk
715	                             factors for muscle injury.
716	
717	                             4.1. Clinical Implications
718	                                   These results emphasize the importance of carefully considering the infection in the
719	                             decision-making process for determining athletes’ readiness to return to sport (RTS). In
720	                             fact, as already described by Elliot et al. [37] in addition to the known complications, it is
721	                             necessary to consider that COVID-19 can be responsible for musculoskeletal complications.
722	                             Therefore, our opinion is that the decision regarding the RTS should not only take into
723	                             account the remission of COVID-19 related symptoms, rest and the cessation of post-
724	                             COVID-19 drug therapy but should include specific assessment and training programs,
725	                             generally used after a musculoskeletal injury [38] and therefore consider COVID-19 not
726	                             only a risk factor but a real injury.
727	
728	                             4.2. Study Limitations
729	                                   One possible limitation of this study is that the muscle injury events were collected
730	                             from a single database, which may have resulted in some injuries being overlooked, omit-
731	                             ted, or interpreted differently, leading to over- or underestimation. Another limitation of
732	                             this study is that it was not possible to control for some factors that may have influenced
733	                             the increased risk of injury, such as previous muscle injuries in unexamined seasons,
734	                             severity of COVID-19-related symptoms, total period of quarantine and injured body
735	                             part. Nevertheless, the study’s strength lies in its design, with a largely homogeneous
736	                             population group of male professional soccer players followed prospectively with a
737	                             standardized methodology.
738	
739	                             5. Conclusions
740	                                  This retrospective cohort study, conducted on a large sample of professional male
741	                             football players from two main European leagues, has revealed a significant association
742	                             between SARS-CoV-2 infection and increased risk of muscular injury. The results of this
743	                             study show that the risk of muscular injury is 3.7 to 5.1 times higher in football players who
744	                             have been infected with SARS-CoV-2. Overall, our study highlights the need for further
745	                             investigation into the effects of SARS-CoV-2 on athletes and the development of tailored
746	                             rehabilitation protocols to ensure a safe return to play.

                                         was conducted to investigate the correlation between SARS-CoV-2 infection and muscle injuries.
                                         Players were divided into two groups based on whether they contracted the SARS-CoV-2 infection
                                         (C+) or not (C−) during the 2020/2021 season. In the 2019–2020 season, both championships showed

                                         higher number of MI compared to C− in both championships (Serie A: p < 0.05; 95% CI 0.731
                                         to 1.038; LaLiga: p < 0.05; 95% CI: 0.773 to 1.054). Multiple linear regression analysis confirmed

Infect. Dis. Rep. 2023, 15, 425–435. https://doi.org/10.3390/idr15040043                                             https://www.mdpi.com/journal/idr
 Infect. Dis. Rep. 2023, 15                                                                                              426




                             on professional athletes, even in mild cases, leading to muscle weakness, poor tolerance to
                             physical exercise, periods of inactivity and absence from sporting practice, with a consider-
                             able impact also on bio-psychosocial context [7–9]. COVID-19 is known to cause severe
                             inflammatory responses, respiratory failure, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS),
                             and bilateral pneumonia [1]; in some cases, these symptoms can continue causing what
                             is called long COVID. It can also affect the musculoskeletal system, causing myalgia and
                             sarcopenia in COVID-19 positive patients [10]. Therefore, the question arises whether
                             COVID-19 may have influenced the number of muscle injuries in elite athletes. Previous
                             studies in the literature have observed that the approximately three months of sports
                             activity suspension due to the lockdown caused an increase in the incidence of injuries
                             in the main European football leagues, including the Bundesliga (Germany) [11], LaLiga
                             (Spain) [12] and Premier League (England) [13]. The only exception is represented by
                             the Italian first division (Serie A) [14], where a non-statistically significant difference was
                             observed between pre- and post-lockdown injuries. However, these studies did not show
                             whether contracting SARS-CoV-2 infection can be considered an additional risk factor for
                             injury occurrence. Only the recent prospective study by Wezenbeek et al. [15] involving
                             three Belgian professional male football teams during the first half of the 2020–2021 season,
                             reported a five-fold higher risk of developing a muscle strain after a SARS-CoV-2 infection.
                             The goal of this study is to further investigate the findings reported by Wezenbeek et al. [15]
                             and to retrospectively examine on a larger sample size, the correlation between SARS-CoV-2
                             infection and muscle injuries among professional football players from two different cham-
                             pionships, Serie A and LaLiga. These two championships were chosen because Serie A was
                             an exception in terms of post-lockdown injury increase, while LaLiga had the most active
                             collaboration in identifying and communicating positive cases and its results were more
                             discordant between pre- and post-lockdown.
                                   However, these studies did not show whether having contracted SARS-CoV-2 infection
                             can be considered an additional risk factor for the occurrence of injuries. Recently only the
                             prospective study by Wezenbeek et al., involving three Belgian professional male football
                             teams, during the first half of the 2020–2021 season reported a five times higher risk of
                             developing a muscle strain after a SARS-CoV-2 infection.
                                   The goal of this study is to deepen the results reported by Wezenbeek et al. and to
                             retrospectively verify, on a larger sample, the correlation between SARS-CoV-2 infection and
                             muscle injuries among professional footballers of two different championship Serie A and
                             LaLiga. The choice of these two different championships was because Serie A represented
                             the exception of post-lockdown injuries increase and both Serie A and LaLiga had the most
                             active collaboration in identifying and communicating positive cases [12]. Our hypothesis
                             is that there is a relationship between muscle injury and previous SARS-CoV-2 infection.

                             2. Materials and Methods
                             2.1. Study Design
                                  A retrospective cohort study was conducted according to the STROBE guidelines [16].
                             The aim was to identify a potential correlation between SARS-CoV-2 infection and muscle
                             injuries in professional soccer players from the Serie A and LaLiga leagues during the
                             2019–2020 and 2020–2021 football seasons. The study included all players from Serie A and
                             LaLiga during the two seasons, as well as those who changed league levels during this
                             time period (e.g., from a minor league such as Serie B in Italy to the top national league,
                             Serie A) and those who moved to a foreign team. Athletes were divided into two groups:
                             COVID-positive (C+) and COVID-negative (C−).
                                  The grouping was performed as follows: (1) all football players infected during the
                             2020–2021 season were classified as “C+”, while all players who did not contract the
                             infection during this time period were classified as “C−”; (2) players who contracted the
                             infection during the 2019–2020 season or during off-season periods (e.g., season summer
                             suspension) were excluded from the study (Serie A n = 29; LaLiga n = 38) and their data
 Infect. Dis. Rep. 2023, 15                                                                                                    427




                             were removed from both seasons. This created a database with pre-COVID (2019–2020
                             season) and post-COVID (2020–2021 season) data.

                             2.2. Data Collection
                                  Data collection was conducted using the Transfermarkt24 site (URL: https://www.
                             transfermarkt.co.uk/, accessed on 12 September 2022) a website founded in Germany in
                             May 2000 which contains a wealth of football information from leagues around the world,
                             including data on the type and severity of injuries. This methodology is consistent with
                             previous studies [17–20]. The data collected are specified in Table 1.

                             2.3. Statistical Analysis
                                    Statistical analysis was performed according to the CHAMP statement [21] using
                             MedCalc software (Version 20, MedCalc Software Ltd., Ostend, Belgium). The normal
                             distribution of the data was verified using the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test. The compar-
                             ison of mean injuries between the two groups in the 2019–2020 and 2020–2021 seasons
                             (i.e., change between seasons) was performed using a parametric t-Student test. A multi-
                             ple linear regression analysis was carried out in both seasons to analyse the relationship
                             between the dependent variable, muscle injuries, and the independent variables of age,
                             SARS-CoV-2 infection, minutes played, and matches played. Additionally, a Kaplan–Meier
                             survival analysis was performed, using the elapsed time (in days) from the start of each
                             championship to the day on which the injury occurred during the in-season period as the
                             “survival time”. If no injuries occurred, the total duration of the season in days was used
                             as the survival time. The Kaplan–Meier curves were analysed using the Logrank Test in
                             both seasons.

                             3. Results
                                  The study included 634 players from Serie A (mean age = 27.9 ± 4.7 years) and
                             649 players from LaLiga (mean age = 28.2 ± 4.2 years), for a total of 1283 elite football
                             players. Of the Italian championship players, 171 (27.3%) were infected with SARS-CoV-2,
                             with 29 excluded due to being infected during the 2019-2020 season. In LaLiga, a total of
                             165 (25.4%) players were infected with SARS-CoV-2, with 38 excluded as they were infected
                             during the 2019–2020 season (Figure 1).

                             4. Discussion
                                   The main aim of this study was to determine whether professional soccer players
                             who contracted SARS-CoV-2 had an increased risk of muscular injuries. The find-
                             ings of this study reported a three to five times increased risk of muscle injury after
                             SARS-CoV-2 infection.
                                   Over the years, UEFA has conducted numerous studies on the match/minute ratio
                             played by the elite athletes of the teams participating in its international tournaments
                             to define a “normal” value for the incidence of injuries in football [22–24]. In particular,
                             Hägglund et al.’s 11-year retrospective study [23] observed the incidence of injuries in more
                             than 1000 h of play and found an incidence of 2 injuries per year per individual footballer
                             or an average of 50 injuries if we take into consideration the team group (list of 25 athletes).
                             If we consider only muscular injuries, the incidence drops to 15 injuries out of a shortlist of
                             25 footballers, with an average per athlete of 0.6 injuries [22]. These data are essential for
                             commenting on the results of our study. Our results showed that in both leagues, players
                             who did not contract COVID-19 had injury rates lower than the average of 0.6 reported by
                             Bengtsson et al. [22] in both seasons. Instead, regarding players infected with SARS-CoV-2,
                             they showed in the pre-COVID season an injury rate in line with the data of Bengtsson
                             et al. [22], while in the 2020/2021 season, after the infection, it increased significantly in
 Infect. Dis. Rep. 2023, 15                                                                                              432




                             both leagues (1.44 for Serie A and 1.23 for LaLiga). The results relating to the change
                             between seasons within individual groups showed significant differences in both groups;
                             however, it should be specified that with such large samples, it is highly probable that even
                             minimal variations between seasons are significant (especially in the C− group which is
                             substantially larger than the C+ group), while if we look at the 95% confidence intervals
                             we see an higher increase in number of injuries in the 2020/2021 season among football
                             players who have had COVID-19.
                                   The results of minutes and matches played showed that in Serie A the players in the
                             C+ group, during the 2019/2020 season, played more games and in total more minutes
                             than the players in group C−; in the 2020/2021 season, the players in group C+ (which
                             contracted COVID-19 during this season), they played fewer games and in total fewer
                             minutes than in the previous season, on the contrary the players in group C− obtained
                             an increase in total games and minutes played. This could be caused both by the period
                             of absence linked to the infection itself and by the greater number of muscle injuries that
                             players in group C+ have suffered, forcing them to have a longer period of absence from
                             sporting activity. The same, albeit to a lesser extent, is observed in the Spanish league
                             showing a substantial overlap of minutes played and games played in the 19/20 season
                             between the two groups; however, in the following season, there was a reduction in minutes
                             and games played in group C+ and an increase in games played and a slight reduction
                             in minutes played in group C−. Our results indicate that SARS-CoV-2 infection could be
                             a risk factor for muscular injury, in line with the recent study by Wezenbeek et al. [15].
                             Multiple linear regression analysis showed that in the 2019–2020 season, the risk of injury
                             was significantly influenced by age, according to a previous study by Green et al. [25].
                             However, in the 2020–2021 season, SARS-CoV-2 infection was the variable that highly
                             influenced the risk of muscle injury. Therefore, belonging to the C+ group in the 2020–2021
                             season completely distorts the correlation between the various variables and the muscle
                             injury rates, becoming the main factor capable of influencing the latter. In other words,
                             while older players with a high number of games and playing time were at greater risk of
                             incurring muscle injuries in the 2019–2020 season, having contracted COVID-19 was the
                             primary and most important risk factor in the following season. Similarly, in LaLiga, age
                             was the main risk factor for muscle injury in the 2019–2020 season, while in the 2020–2021
                             season, the only variable that significantly influenced muscle injuries was the SARS-CoV-2
                             infection. The survival analysis showed that during the 2019–2020 season, the two groups
                             had a similar risk of muscular injury. In the 2020/2021 season, the hazard risk ratio was 3.7
                             to 5.1 times greater among those athletes infected by SARS-CoV-2, in line with the results
                             of Wezenbeek et al. [15], which reported a five-time higher hazard rate to develop a muscle
                             strain after SARS-CoV-2 infection. One of the reasons that could explain the age effect only
                             in the Italian league and not in the Spanish may depend on the fact that age is a variable
                             not always correlated to injury. In fact, a recent review [26] reported that age influences
                             athletes’ risk of calf muscle injuries, while another review [27] showed that age is not linked
                             to a higher risk of quadriceps muscle injury. Nevertheless, the source of our data is not
                             specific to the type of injury and therefore it was not possible to carry out a sub-analysis.
                             Future studies will have to consider this element to draw definitive conclusions regarding
                             the role of age on the risk of injuries.
                                   As discussed by Wezenbeek et al. [15], there are two possible explanations for the
                             correlation between SARS-CoV-2 infection and an increased risk of muscular injury. The
                             first hypothesis is that strict quarantine rules implemented during the 2020/2021 season
                             led to prolonged periods of abstention from training and sports participation, resulting in
                             muscular detraining [28,29] and subsequent loss of muscle strength [30]. Muscle strength
                             has been shown to be a protective factor against muscular injury [31], and the loss of muscle
                             strength is more significant in highly trained athletes with greater initial muscle mass [32].
                             The second explanation is related to the direct biological effects of the virus. SARS-CoV-2
                             infection causes hyperinflammation, an increase in inflammatory markers, an increase
                             in the neutrophil/lymphocyte ratio, and possible depletion of circulating T cells [33].
 Infect. Dis. Rep. 2023, 15                                                                                                      433




                             Furthermore, the virus may cause direct damage to muscle tissue by targeting the ACE 2
                             receptor [17], which is widely present in muscle tissue [34]. In addition, the virus can cause
                             disturbances in blood flow and oxygen transport, leading to reduced muscle oxygenation
                             during exercise. Lower muscle oxygen saturation [35] and VO2 max [36] are possible risk
                             factors for muscle injury.

                             4.1. Clinical Implications
                                   These results emphasize the importance of carefully considering the infection in the
                             decision-making process for determining athletes’ readiness to return to sport (RTS). In
                             fact, as already described by Elliot et al. [37] in addition to the known complications, it is
                             necessary to consider that COVID-19 can be responsible for musculoskeletal complications.
                             Therefore, our opinion is that the decision regarding the RTS should not only take into
                             account the remission of COVID-19 related symptoms, rest and the cessation of post-
                             COVID-19 drug therapy but should include specific assessment and training programs,
                             generally used after a musculoskeletal injury [38] and therefore consider COVID-19 not
                             only a risk factor but a real injury.

                             4.2. Study Limitations
                                   One possible limitation of this study is that the muscle injury events were collected
                             from a single database, which may have resulted in some injuries being overlooked, omit-
                             ted, or interpreted differently, leading to over- or underestimation. Another limitation of
                             this study is that it was not possible to control for some factors that may have influenced
                             the increased risk of injury, such as previous muscle injuries in unexamined seasons,
                             severity of COVID-19-related symptoms, total period of quarantine and injured body
                             part. Nevertheless, the study’s strength lies in its design, with a largely homogeneous
                             population group of male professional soccer players followed prospectively with a
                             standardized methodology.

                             5. Conclusions
                                  This retrospective cohort study, conducted on a large sample of professional male
                             football players from two main European leagues, has revealed a significant association
                             between SARS-CoV-2 infection and increased risk of muscular injury. The results of this
                             study show that the risk of muscular injury is 3.7 to 5.1 times higher in football players who
                             have been infected with SARS-CoV-2. Overall, our study highlights the need for further
                             investigation into the effects of SARS-CoV-2 on athletes and the development of tailored
                             rehabilitation protocols to ensure a safe return to play.

1	Speeding Up or Slowing Down: The Effect of
2	Decoupling Speed on Knee Biomechanics
3	and Limb Loading During Split-Belt
4	Treadmill Training in Persons With ACL
5	Reconstruction
6	Alexa K. Johnson,* PhD, Reagan Recchia,* BS, Abdulhamit Tayfur,*y PT, PhD,
7	Chandramouli Krishnan,z§||{# PT, PhD, and Riann M. Palmieri-Smith,*#** ATC, PhD
8	Investigation performed at University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA
9	
10	Background: Surgical limb underloading is a common biomechanical adaptation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction
11	(ACLR) and has been linked to early degenerative changes in knee cartilage, which are considered precursors to posttraumatic
12	osteoarthritis. Split-belt treadmill training is an emerging rehabilitation approach that modifies load through asymmetric gait
13	behavior, in which one limb walks faster than the other. While previous research has indicated that split-belt treadmill training
14	can modify limb loading, its effects on post-ACLR biomechanics remain unexplored.
15	Purpose/Hypothesis: The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of decoupling speed on knee biomechanics and limb
16	loading and model their relationship. It was hypothesized that at faster decoupling speeds, knee loads would increase, and at
17	slower speeds, they would decrease.
18	Study Design: Controlled laboratory study.
19	Methods: Knee joint biomechanics were evaluated while 24 participants (15 females; mean age, 23.5 6 6.5 years; mean height,
20	1.72 6 0.08 m; mean mass, 75.61 6 13.83 kg; mean postoperative time, 7.94 6 1.74 months) with ACLR walked on an instru-
21	mented treadmill (2000 Hz) synced with a 12-camera motion capture system (200 Hz). Participants completed 5 minutes of base-
22	line walking at 1.1 m/s on tied treadmill belts. Afterward, the authors manipulated the speed of the belt under the ACL-
23	reconstructed leg with 8 randomized 5-minute decoupled speed configurations (ACL-reconstructed limb at 30%-170% of
24	1.1 m/s in 20% increments) with 2 minutes of tied-belt walking between each speed. Bilateral sagittal plane knee moments,
25	angles, and vertical ground-reaction forces were calculated. Statistical parametric mapping was used to evaluate the effects
26	of decoupling speed on the dependent variables during the stance phase of the gait.
27	Results: A clear dose-response relationship between decoupling speed and knee/limb loading was found. Specifically, faster de-
28	coupling speeds (130%-170% of 1.1m/s) generally increased peak loads and slower speeds (30% and 50% of 1.1 m/s) decreased
29	peak loads during early stance compared with tied-belt walking for both limbs. In contrast, slower decoupling speeds (30%-90% of
30	1.1 m/s) led to higher bilateral knee/limb loads at midstance, while faster decoupling speeds (130%-170% of 1.1 m/s) resulted in
31	less knee/limb loading during midstance.
32	Conclusion: These findings suggest that split-belt treadmill training offers a promising method for modulating knee/limb loading
33	post-ACLR.
34	Clinical Relevance: Split-belt treadmill training could be a viable intervention to target the loading asymmetry that is prevalent in
35	persons post-ACLR.
36	Keywords: knee; rehabilitation; gait retraining; asymmetry

Speeding Up or Slowing Down: The Effect of
Decoupling Speed on Knee Biomechanics
and Limb Loading During Split-Belt
Treadmill Training in Persons With ACL
Reconstruction
Alexa K. Johnson,* PhD, Reagan Recchia,* BS, Abdulhamit Tayfur,*y PT, PhD,
Chandramouli Krishnan,z§||{# PT, PhD, and Riann M. Palmieri-Smith,*#** ATC, PhD
Investigation performed at University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, Michigan, USA

Background: Surgical limb underloading is a common biomechanical adaptation after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction
(ACLR) and has been linked to early degenerative changes in knee cartilage, which are considered precursors to posttraumatic
osteoarthritis. Split-belt treadmill training is an emerging rehabilitation approach that modifies load through asymmetric gait
behavior, in which one limb walks faster than the other. While previous research has indicated that split-belt treadmill training
can modify limb loading, its effects on post-ACLR biomechanics remain unexplored.
Purpose/Hypothesis: The purpose of this study was to examine the effects of decoupling speed on knee biomechanics and limb
loading and model their relationship. It was hypothesized that at faster decoupling speeds, knee loads would increase, and at
slower speeds, they would decrease.
Study Design: Controlled laboratory study.
Methods: Knee joint biomechanics were evaluated while 24 participants (15 females; mean age, 23.5 6 6.5 years; mean height,
1.72 6 0.08 m; mean mass, 75.61 6 13.83 kg; mean postoperative time, 7.94 6 1.74 months) with ACLR walked on an instru-
mented treadmill (2000 Hz) synced with a 12-camera motion capture system (200 Hz). Participants completed 5 minutes of base-
line walking at 1.1 m/s on tied treadmill belts. Afterward, the authors manipulated the speed of the belt under the ACL-
reconstructed leg with 8 randomized 5-minute decoupled speed configurations (ACL-reconstructed limb at 30%-170% of
1.1 m/s in 20% increments) with 2 minutes of tied-belt walking between each speed. Bilateral sagittal plane knee moments,
angles, and vertical ground-reaction forces were calculated. Statistical parametric mapping was used to evaluate the effects
of decoupling speed on the dependent variables during the stance phase of the gait.
Results: A clear dose-response relationship between decoupling speed and knee/limb loading was found. Specifically, faster de-
coupling speeds (130%-170% of 1.1m/s) generally increased peak loads and slower speeds (30% and 50% of 1.1 m/s) decreased
peak loads during early stance compared with tied-belt walking for both limbs. In contrast, slower decoupling speeds (30%-90% of
1.1 m/s) led to higher bilateral knee/limb loads at midstance, while faster decoupling speeds (130%-170% of 1.1 m/s) resulted in
less knee/limb loading during midstance.
Conclusion: These findings suggest that split-belt treadmill training offers a promising method for modulating knee/limb loading
post-ACLR.
Clinical Relevance: Split-belt treadmill training could be a viable intervention to target the loading asymmetry that is prevalent in
persons post-ACLR.
Keywords: knee; rehabilitation; gait retraining; asymmetry

15	Abstract
16	Carnosine levels play a significant role in intracellular pH buffering during exercise. The limiting factor for muscle carno-
17	sine synthesis is the availability of β-alanine. Results from meta-analysis showed a significant positive effect of β-alanine
18	supplementation on high-intensity exercise performance. Nonetheless, much less has been described about the safety of
19	β-alanine. The available literature indicates no adverse events related to β-alanine usage; side effects such as paresthesia
20	may be observed if a large single high dose of β-alanine is taken, but the symptom can be attenuated either by using splitting
21	doses (< 1.6 g) or a sustained-release formula. No adverse effects have been reported up to 24 weeks of β-alanine supple-
22	mentation (3.2 g.day−1), but the adverse effects of longer supplementation periods are still unknown. Most of the existing
23	clinical studies were not designed with safety evaluations as primary end points. β-Alanine is currently considered to be safe
24	in healthy populations, at recommended doses, by the International Society of Sports Nutrition stands position, while the
25	Australian Institute of Sports has established β-alanine as a safe performance-enhancing supplement with strong scientific
26	evidence (grade A). Cohort studies are needed evaluating the safety of β-alanine among representative populations, and the
27	effects of co-variables such as sex, age, and ethnicity.

    REVIEW



Safety of beta‑alanine supplementation in humans: a narrative review
Erick P. de Oliveira1 · Guilherme G. Artioli2 · Roberto Carlos Burini3

Received: 12 June 2022 / Accepted: 8 February 2023
© The Author(s), under exclusive licence to Springer-Verlag Italia S.r.l., part of Springer Nature 2023


Abstract
Carnosine levels play a significant role in intracellular pH buffering during exercise. The limiting factor for muscle carno-
sine synthesis is the availability of β-alanine. Results from meta-analysis showed a significant positive effect of β-alanine
supplementation on high-intensity exercise performance. Nonetheless, much less has been described about the safety of
β-alanine. The available literature indicates no adverse events related to β-alanine usage; side effects such as paresthesia
may be observed if a large single high dose of β-alanine is taken, but the symptom can be attenuated either by using splitting
doses (< 1.6 g) or a sustained-release formula. No adverse effects have been reported up to 24 weeks of β-alanine supple-
mentation (3.2 g.day−1), but the adverse effects of longer supplementation periods are still unknown. Most of the existing
clinical studies were not designed with safety evaluations as primary end points. β-Alanine is currently considered to be safe
in healthy populations, at recommended doses, by the International Society of Sports Nutrition stands position, while the
Australian Institute of Sports has established β-alanine as a safe performance-enhancing supplement with strong scientific
evidence (grade A). Cohort studies are needed evaluating the safety of β-alanine among representative populations, and the
effects of co-variables such as sex, age, and ethnicity.

Keywords Safety · Adverse events · Side effects · Exercise · Performance

16	Abstract
17	   As the NFL's salary cap has surged from $34 million in 1994 to $255 million in 2024, effective cap
18	management has become crucial. However, relatively little focus has been paid to how spending on spe-
19	cific positions affects team success. The purpose of this study was to examine the relationship between
20	salary cap allocation and team success in the NFL, specifically focusing on how spending in different
21	positions affects win percentage. We utilized a quantitative design, analyzing 384 NFL team observations
22	from the 2013–2024 seasons, with linear regression models applied to assess how salary cap allocations
23	across key positions impacted team success, using win percentage as the primary outcome variable and
24	the number of wins as a robustness check. Our findings show that higher spending on quarterbacks, wide
25	receivers, and offensive linemen is strongly linked to improved team performance, while expenditures
26	on running backs and tight ends have little to no significant impact. These results suggest that teams
27	could benefit from reallocating resources to more critical positions, particularly quarterbacks and wide
28	receivers, to maximize on-field performance. This study also offers practical insights for NFL teams
29	seeking to refine their salary cap strategies.

Salary dispersion and team success: The impact of po-
sitional spending on win percentage in the National
Football League
                                                                                Heimo Schaflechner
                                                                                 Texas Tech University
                                                                                       Hoyoon Jung
                                                                                 Texas Tech University

Abstract
   As the NFL's salary cap has surged from $34 million in 1994 to $255 million in 2024, effective cap
management has become crucial. However, relatively little focus has been paid to how spending on spe-
cific positions affects team success. The purpose of this study was to examine the relationship between
salary cap allocation and team success in the NFL, specifically focusing on how spending in different
positions affects win percentage. We utilized a quantitative design, analyzing 384 NFL team observations
from the 2013–2024 seasons, with linear regression models applied to assess how salary cap allocations
across key positions impacted team success, using win percentage as the primary outcome variable and
the number of wins as a robustness check. Our findings show that higher spending on quarterbacks, wide
receivers, and offensive linemen is strongly linked to improved team performance, while expenditures
on running backs and tight ends have little to no significant impact. These results suggest that teams
could benefit from reallocating resources to more critical positions, particularly quarterbacks and wide
receivers, to maximize on-field performance. This study also offers practical insights for NFL teams

99	Abstract:
100	Background: Sport-related concussion (SRC) prevention and management is a focus of the
101	National Football League (NFL). While most prior reports evaluate SRC incidence, few have
102	studied same-year repeat concussions. The objective of this study was to evaluate the frequency
103	of same-year repeat concussions in the NFL.
104	Methods: A retrospective, case-control study of same-year repeat concussion in the NFL from
105	2015-2019 was performed. The electronic health record of the NFL was reviewed for players
106	sustaining concussions and same-year repeat concussions. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were used to
107	calculate same-year repeat concussion rates, and risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals (CIs)
108	were estimated using log-binomial regression.               of
109	Results: From 2015-2019, the risk of sustaining a same-year repeat concussion in the NFL
110	                                                      ro
111	ranged from 0.38% to 0.69% per season. Among players who sustained a concussion, the risk of
112	                                                -p
113	a same-year repeat concussion ranged from 5.3% to 8.3%, which did not differ significantly from
114	
115	                                          re
116	the risk of sustaining a single concussion, which ranged from 6.2% to 8.3%. There was a median
117	of 38 participation days between initial and same-year repeat concussion. Players missed more
118	                                   lP
119	time from same-year repeat concussion (median 12 days) compared to both single (median 9
120	
121	                           na
122	days; p<0.0001) and initial (median 9.5 days, p=0.002) concussions.
123	Conclusions: The risk of a repeat concussion was similar to the risk of sustaining a single
124	                      ur
125	concussion among NFL players. More time was missed following a same-year repeat concussion
126	
127	               Jo
128	compared to single or initial concussions. Further research is needed to maximize player safety
129	and minimize same-year repeat concussions.

138	Introduction
139	       Increasing knowledge and awareness surrounding sport-related concussion (SRC) in
140	recent decades has resulted in concerted efforts directed toward reducing repeat SRC rates.
141	Repeat or recurrent concussions have been associated with a slower recovery,1 depression,2 sleep
142	disturbances,3 late-life cognitive impairment,4 and longer return-to-play (RTP) times compared
143	to first-time injuries.5,6,7 Though many studies have evaluated the risk of repeat SRC throughout
144	an athlete’s career,2,4,8–10 few have delved into the incidence of same-year repeat concussions,
145	especially among elite American football players.
146	       A previous study reviewed concussions in the National Football League (NFL) between
147	
148	                                                             of
149	1996 and 2001 and reported a 5.5% rate of same-season repeat concussions.11 A follow-up study
150	found a similar risk of repeat concussions between two time periods of the 1996-2001 vs. 2002-
151	                                                       ro
152	2007 seasons (24.7% vs. 24.2%).11 Although the second follow-up study did not restrict the
153	                                                 -p
154	definition of repeat concussion to same-year repeat concussion, the authors found that 90% of
155	
156	                                           re
157	repeat concussions occurred more than 28 days after the initial concussion. The average time
158	between concussions was 456 days, signifying most injuries likely occurred in different
159	seasons.11                         lP
160	                            na
161	       Several evidence-based changes in concussion detection and RTP protocols have been
162	implemented in the NFL in recent years.12–14 With respect to RTP, players must pass a series of
163	                      ur
164	clinical qualifications to be cleared for play. From 2015-2019, between 283-302 concussions
165	
166	               Jo
167	were reported per year (offseason through the postseason) in the NFL.15 The most recent
168	publication regarding same-year repeat concussion in the NFL is from 1996-2001;16 more recent
169	data is needed to fully understand the current scope of same-year repeat concussion.
170	       In the current study, we sought to: 1) report the risk of same-year repeat concussions in
171	the NFL, 2) describe the time pattern of when same-year repeat concussions occur, and 3)
172	present RTP time and intervening time between same-year repeat concussions. Given recent
173	evidence-based changes in concussion management, the staged approach for RTP, and plateaued
174	rates of SRC due to increased awareness and prevention measures,15 we would expect the risk of
175	same-year repeat concussion in the NFL to have plateaued from previous studies.

185	Research Design
186	       A retrospective, observational cohort study of NFL players during the 2015 through 2019
187	seasons was conducted in accordance with the NFL and National Football League Players
188	Association (NFLPA) Medical and Scientific Research Protocol Approval Process17 and was
189	approved by the [blinded for review] institutional review board (0006018120). Medical records
190	of all players with football-related concussions were reviewed for this study.

197	seasons were included. All NFL-related concussions were included, regardless of severity,

214	through mid-March and is denoted by the initial year. The year begins with an offseason program
215	and progresses in order of preseason, regular season, and postseason. An initial concussion was
216	defined as the first concussion in a player who sustained a same-year repeat concussion. A player
217	with a single concussion was defined as a player who had only one concussion during the full

223	number of days between removal from participation due to the concussion and return to full

336	Discussion
337	       This study aimed to summarize the risk of same-year repeat concussion in NFL players
338	over 5 seasons. From 2015-2019, the risk of any NFL player sustaining a same-year repeat
339	concussion ranged from 0.38% to 0.69%. In players sustaining at least one concussion, the risk
340	of sustaining a same-year repeat concussion was 5.3% to 8.3%, which was similar to the risk of
341	sustaining at least one concussion at 6.2% to 8.0%. Time missed for the same-year repeat
342	concussion was longer than for a single concussion (12 vs. 9 days). A trend toward higher risk of
343	same-year repeat concussion was seen in players who missed 8 or more days after the initial
344	concussion, though this trend was not significant.
345	
346	                                                              of
347	       Few studies have evaluated the risk of same-year repeat concussion at any level, and only
348	two studies at the NFL level exist. From 1996-2001, Pellman et al.16 reported that of 650 players
349	                                                        ro
350	who sustained a concussion, 36 (5.5%) sustained at least one same-season repeat concussion,
351	                                                  -p
352	which is similar to the 7.0% reported in this study. One explanation for the small difference is
353	
354	                                            re
355	the inclusion of the off-season in our study, which accounted for two of the initial concussions in
356	the same-year concussion group. Unfortunately, Pellman et al. did not report the risk of same-
357	                                    lP
358	season repeat concussion for all NFL players in that time period, which in the current study was
359	
360	                            na
361	low at 0.51%.16 Casson, et al.11 compared the data from the 1996-2001 and 2001-2006 seasons
362	and found that the risk of repeat concussions – more than one concussion in the study window
363	                      ur
364	and not same-season repeat concussion – remained similar across the two time periods (24.7%
365	
366	               Jo
367	vs. 24.2%, respectively). While that study did not specifically report same-season repeat
368	concussions, it did note that the majority of players (89.8%) had more than 28 days between
369	concussions (average 456 days), with only 2.8% experiencing a repeat concussion within the
370	same week.11
371	       Since the publication of these early studies, and prior to the initial years of the current
372	study, several policy changes have been implemented regarding the management of concussed
373	players in the NFL, including indicators for immediate removal from play, a stepwise RTP
374	protocol, and mandatory evaluation by an independent neurological consultant.14 In the current
375	study, no player sustained a repeat concussion within 13 days of onset of the initial concussion.
376	Mack, et al., found that the concussion risk declined significantly in the 2018-2019 seasons
377	(6.2% and 7.1%, respectively) compared to the 2015-2017 seasons (7.4%-8.3%), thought to be
378	attributed to a dedicated focus on concussion awareness prior to the 2018 season.15 Additional
379	
380	
381	
382	                                                                                                     6
383	                                                                                                Cools

385	
386	rule changes after 2018 included elimination of blind-side blocks and updated kickoff rules.
387	Helmets were also tested in the laboratory,18 the results of which were made available to players
388	and teams. A subsequent policy mandated that players choose among higher performing helmets,
389	with poorer performing helmets being banned. Our data on same-year repeat concussions in the
390	same time interval do not demonstrate a significant decrease in the rate of same-year repeat
391	concussions, though 2019 did have the lowest rate (0.38%). This is likely due to the relatively
392	low numbers of same-year repeat concussions and a decrease in the denominator of overall
393	concussions.
394	        Same-year repeat concussions at the collegiate level also warrant discussion in the
395	
396	                                                             of
397	context of elite American football. The National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA)
398	Concussion study (1999-2001) by Guskiewicz, et al.1 found a 6.5% risk of same-season repeat
399	                                                       ro
400	concussion among football players. In these athletes, the median RTP was 3.0 days and 91% of
401	                                                 -p
402	repeat concussions occurred within 10 days of the initial concussion. A subsequent study
403	
404	                                           re
405	involving the Concussion Assessment, Research, and Education (CARE) Consortium, collecting
406	data from 2014-2017,6 found a same-season repeat concussion rate of 3.9%, demonstrating a
407	                                    lP
408	significant decline from the initial NCAA Concussion Study. RTP time was longer in the CARE
409	
410	                            na
411	Consortium compared to the 1999-2001 study (median 12.2 days) and only 3.7% of same-season
412	repeat concussions occurred within 10 days of the initial concussion.6 Though comparisons
413	                      ur
414	between playing levels are made cautiously, the current NFL data demonstrate a higher risk of
415	
416	                Jo
417	same-year season repeat concussion (6.8%) in NFL players compared to the CARE consortium
418	cohort of collegiate football players (3.9%).6,19 One explanation for higher risk of same-year
419	repeat concussion may be differences in the length of the study period. The current study
420	included the full NFL year (offseason, 4 preseason games, 16 regular season games, and
421	potential for 4 postseason games), which is longer than a NCAA season. The NCAA football
422	season typically runs from the beginning of workouts in July through late December or early
423	January bowl games, with between 12 and 1 games for most teams. Other explanations may
424	include differences in the style of play, access and availability of medical care, motivations for
425	RTP, differences in data collection, or other differences between collegiate and professional
426	football settings.
427	        The current study suggests that the risk of sustaining a same-year repeat concussion is
428	similar to the risk of sustaining a single concussion. Stable rates of same-year repeat and single

437	return from their injuries and re-enter the population at risk with a similar risk of sustaining a
438	concussion, rather than having an elevated risk for a repeat concussion. Hypothetically, if an
439	elevated risk of same-year repeat concussion compared to single concussions were to be found,
440	this may indicate a potential premature RTP following the initial concussion. Premature RTP has
441	been associated with a risk of additional concussion and a prolonged recovery,1 in addition to an
442	increased risk of musculoskeletal injury,20–22 or even second impact syndrome.23,24
443	       RTP times in our cohort were longer with repeat concussions (median 12 days) compared
444	to single concussions (median 9 days), which is also consistent with several previous studies

447	demonstrating prolonged recovery time from repeat concussions in high-school,25,26 collegiate,1,6
448	and professional27 sports. Though the current study cannot assess causation, these data may
449	                                                        ro
450	indicate that a second concussion within the same season may result in an injury requiring more

452	recovery time. An alternative possibility is that team physicians and athletic trainers tend to be

471	       This study has limitations. This study focused on two or more concussions within an NFL
472	season; it did not evaluate concussions across multiple seasons or incorporate head injuries prior
473	to joining the NFL. It is possible that players had sustained one or more concussions prior to the
474	2015 season in or outside of the NFL, or sustained concussions across multiple seasons within
475	the study. Additionally, same-year repeat concussions may have been impacted by the timing of
476	the initial concussion within the season. For example, if a player sustained a concussion in the
477	latter portion of the year, they would have less time to sustain a same-year repeat concussion, as
478	there would be fewer opportunities to do so with the time remaining in the season. Conversely, a

487	sustain a same-year repeat concussion. Similarly, time to return to participation may have been
488	influenced by timing in the season and other factors. Notably, this analysis does not account for
489	granular time at risk for injury (e.g. player-games or player-days) as participation data outside of
490	games in limited. Also, our data do not account for limitations (e.g. play count or rep maximum)
491	placed on players by coaches, trainers, or athletes themselves once they are cleared for full
492	participation. However, investigating each NFL year as a unique interval allows for the study of
493	same-year risk for repeat concussion, which has not been reported since the newest iteration of
494	the NFL concussion protocols. The small number of same-year repeat concussions limits the

502	Conclusions
503	                                            re
504	                                    lP
505	       This study investigates the risk of same-year repeat concussion in the NFL over 5 seasons
506	
507	                            na
508	from 2015 through 2019. Repeat concussions occurred at a similar rate to initial concussions,
509	indicating that players may not be at increased risk for a subsequent concussion when following
510	                      ur
511	evidence-informed RTP protocols. More missed time from an initial concussion was associated
512	
513	               Jo
514	with an increased risk of repeat concussion, suggesting that a more severe concussion may be
515	associated with an increased risk of subsequent concussion. This study highlights the
516	effectiveness of a robust concussion identification system and RTP protocol. Physicians involved
517	in the evaluation and management of concussion should continue to pay significant attention to
518	the systems of identification of concussion, as well as their RTP protocols. Future research
519	should address risk factors for sustaining repeat concussions in order to enhance player safety.

Corresponding Author and Reprint Requests:

Scott L. Zuckerman, MD, MPH
Department of Neurological Surgery

Nashville, TN 37212

Phone: 914-980-3339 Fax: 615-343-6948
