Key Words: concussion, injury prevention, NFL, real-world evidence, sport-related concussion
              Jo
Short Title: Repeat Concussions in the NFL
                                                                                               Cools


Abstract:
Background: Sport-related concussion (SRC) prevention and management is a focus of the
National Football League (NFL). While most prior reports evaluate SRC incidence, few have
studied same-year repeat concussions. The objective of this study was to evaluate the frequency
of same-year repeat concussions in the NFL.
Methods: A retrospective, case-control study of same-year repeat concussion in the NFL from
2015-2019 was performed. The electronic health record of the NFL was reviewed for players
sustaining concussions and same-year repeat concussions. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were used to
calculate same-year repeat concussion rates, and risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals (CIs)
were estimated using log-binomial regression.               of
Results: From 2015-2019, the risk of sustaining a same-year repeat concussion in the NFL
                                                      ro
ranged from 0.38% to 0.69% per season. Among players who sustained a concussion, the risk of
                                                -p
a same-year repeat concussion ranged from 5.3% to 8.3%, which did not differ significantly from

                                          re
the risk of sustaining a single concussion, which ranged from 6.2% to 8.3%. There was a median
of 38 participation days between initial and same-year repeat concussion. Players missed more
                                   lP
time from same-year repeat concussion (median 12 days) compared to both single (median 9

                           na
days; p<0.0001) and initial (median 9.5 days, p=0.002) concussions.
Conclusions: The risk of a repeat concussion was similar to the risk of sustaining a single
                      ur
concussion among NFL players. More time was missed following a same-year repeat concussion

               Jo
compared to single or initial concussions. Further research is needed to maximize player safety
and minimize same-year repeat concussions.




                                                                                                  1
                                                                                               Cools


Introduction
       Increasing knowledge and awareness surrounding sport-related concussion (SRC) in
recent decades has resulted in concerted efforts directed toward reducing repeat SRC rates.
Repeat or recurrent concussions have been associated with a slower recovery,1 depression,2 sleep
disturbances,3 late-life cognitive impairment,4 and longer return-to-play (RTP) times compared
to first-time injuries.5,6,7 Though many studies have evaluated the risk of repeat SRC throughout
an athlete’s career,2,4,8–10 few have delved into the incidence of same-year repeat concussions,
especially among elite American football players.
       A previous study reviewed concussions in the National Football League (NFL) between

                                                             of
1996 and 2001 and reported a 5.5% rate of same-season repeat concussions.11 A follow-up study
found a similar risk of repeat concussions between two time periods of the 1996-2001 vs. 2002-
                                                       ro
2007 seasons (24.7% vs. 24.2%).11 Although the second follow-up study did not restrict the
                                                 -p
definition of repeat concussion to same-year repeat concussion, the authors found that 90% of

                                           re
repeat concussions occurred more than 28 days after the initial concussion. The average time
between concussions was 456 days, signifying most injuries likely occurred in different
seasons.11                         lP
                            na
       Several evidence-based changes in concussion detection and RTP protocols have been
implemented in the NFL in recent years.12–14 With respect to RTP, players must pass a series of
                      ur
clinical qualifications to be cleared for play. From 2015-2019, between 283-302 concussions

               Jo
were reported per year (offseason through the postseason) in the NFL.15 The most recent
publication regarding same-year repeat concussion in the NFL is from 1996-2001;16 more recent
data is needed to fully understand the current scope of same-year repeat concussion.
       In the current study, we sought to: 1) report the risk of same-year repeat concussions in
the NFL, 2) describe the time pattern of when same-year repeat concussions occur, and 3)
present RTP time and intervening time between same-year repeat concussions. Given recent
evidence-based changes in concussion management, the staged approach for RTP, and plateaued
rates of SRC due to increased awareness and prevention measures,15 we would expect the risk of
same-year repeat concussion in the NFL to have plateaued from previous studies.




                                                                                                    2
                                                                                                Cools


Methods
Research Design
       A retrospective, observational cohort study of NFL players during the 2015 through 2019
seasons was conducted in accordance with the NFL and National Football League Players
Association (NFLPA) Medical and Scientific Research Protocol Approval Process17 and was
approved by the [blinded for review] institutional review board (0006018120). Medical records
of all players with football-related concussions were reviewed for this study.


Participants

                                                              of
       All players who sustained at least one concussion during the 2015 through 2019 NFL
seasons were included. All NFL-related concussions were included, regardless of severity,
                                                        ro
timing within the season, or activity when the injury occurred. Player position was categorized
                                                  -p
by position at time of concussion, with all players injured on special teams plays categorized as a

                                            re
special teams player, rather than by specific roster position: offensive line, running back, tight
end, quarterback, wide receiver, defensive secondary, defensive line, linebacker, or special teams
(e.g. kicker, punter, long snapper).   lP
Data Collection
                            na
                      ur
       A player sustaining a same-year repeat concussion was defined as a player with a second

               Jo
concussion at any point during the same NFL year. An “NFL year” runs from mid-March
through mid-March and is denoted by the initial year. The year begins with an offseason program
and progresses in order of preseason, regular season, and postseason. An initial concussion was
defined as the first concussion in a player who sustained a same-year repeat concussion. A player
with a single concussion was defined as a player who had only one concussion during the full
NFL year (no subsequent concussions in that same year).
       Several time points were considered when evaluating RTP and intervening time between
SRCs. RTP was defined as the time when the athlete had fully cleared concussion protocol and
was released to full-contact practice and games. Any limitations placed on a player meant they
were still completing the concussion protocol and had not yet returned. Missed time was the
number of days between removal from participation due to the concussion and return to full
participation in football activities, exclusive of removal and return dates. Participation days was



                                                                                                     3
                                                                                             Cools


defined as the number of intervening days between full RTP to football activities and the onset
date of the second concussion for players with a same-year repeat concussion, inclusive of both
the return date and the onset date of the second concussion. Additional concussions after the
second were not included when calculating missed time. A schematic depicting key timepoints
among players with same-year repeat concussions is seen in Figure 1.


Statistical Analysis
       Continuous data are presented as median, range, and interquartile range due to skewness
of days missed. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests were used to compare medians. Count data are

                                                            of
presented as n (%). One-season risk was calculated in two ways: 1) the risk of a concussion or
same-year repeat concussion among all players in the NFL, which was calculated as the number
                                                      ro
of players with a concussion divided by the total number of players under contract each full NFL
                                                -p
season, and 2) the risk of a same-year repeat concussion among players who had at least one

                                          re
concussion. Risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated using log-binomial
regression. Significance was considered at alpha of 0.05. All statistical analyses were performed
                                   lP
in SAS 9.4 (SAS Institute, Cary, NC).


Results
                           na
                       ur
Risk of Same-Year Repeat Concussions

               Jo
       The total number of concussions and same-year repeat concussions is presented in Table
1. Among all players, the risk of sustaining a same-year repeat concussion ranged from 0.38% in
2019 to 0.69% in 2017. For those sustaining at least one concussion during an NFL year, the risk
of same-year repeat concussion ranged from 5.3% (2019) to 8.3% (2017). This was similar to the
risk of sustaining any concussion, which ranged from 6.2% (2018) to 8.3% (2017).


Characteristics of Players with Same-Year Repeat Concussions
       Rates of same-year repeat concussions by position at time of concussion were similar
(Table 2). Notable trends include players on special teams plays and in the defensive secondary,
who sustained the largest proportions of both repeat and single concussions. Percentages
comparing single concussions to same-year repeat concussions differed among: 1) tight ends
who sustained 7.9% of single concussions but 12.0% of repeat concussions, 2) wide receivers



                                                                                                  4
                                                                                             Cools


who sustained 12.0% of single concussions but 16.9% of repeat concussions, and 3) offensive
linemen who sustained 17.8% of single concussions but 10.8% of repeat concussions.


Timing of Same-Year Repeat Concussions
       Among 83 players with same-year repeat concussions, 48% (n=40) experienced the first
concussion during the offseason or preseason, and 82% (n=68) had concussions that occurred
during at least one preseason and one regular season or two regular season injuries (Figure 2).


Participation Days Between Injuries

                                                            of
       Players participated a median of 38 days between the first and same-year repeat
concussions (Table 3). The minimum was two days, and maximum was 150 days. In 18.8% of
                                                      ro
players sustaining a same-year repeat concussion, the second concussion occurred within two
                                                -p
weeks of return from the initial concussion. There were three players who sustained a same-year

                                          re
repeat concussion two participation days after returning from the initial concussion. Among
those three cases, the missed time for the initial concussion ranged from 11-19 days, and the
                                   lP
same-year repeat concussions occurred during a regular season game (n=2) or preseason practice

                           na
(n=1). Out of 83 players with a same-year repeat concussion, 55 (66.3%) sustained the second
concussion 36 or more days after the initial concussion; 18 (21.7%) sustained the second
                      ur
concussion 22-35 days after the initial concussion; and the remaining 10 (12.0%) sustained the

                 Jo
concussion 14-21 days after the initial concussion.


Return-to-Play
       Missed time due to first and same-year repeat concussion is seen in Table 4. Missed
time following single concussions (median 9 days) was similar to missed time following initial
concussions (median 9.5 days) (p=0.20); however, missed time after a same-year repeat
concussion was longer (median 12 days) than both single (p<0.0001) and initial (p=0.002)
concussions. Players who missed 8 or more days following their initial concussion trended
toward a higher risk of same-year repeat concussion compared to players who missed 7 or fewer
days from the initial concussion (8.5% vs. 4.9%; RR=1.48, 95% CI 0.94, 2.31, p=0.09).




                                                                                                  5
                                                                                                 Cools


Discussion
       This study aimed to summarize the risk of same-year repeat concussion in NFL players
over 5 seasons. From 2015-2019, the risk of any NFL player sustaining a same-year repeat
concussion ranged from 0.38% to 0.69%. In players sustaining at least one concussion, the risk
of sustaining a same-year repeat concussion was 5.3% to 8.3%, which was similar to the risk of
sustaining at least one concussion at 6.2% to 8.0%. Time missed for the same-year repeat
concussion was longer than for a single concussion (12 vs. 9 days). A trend toward higher risk of
same-year repeat concussion was seen in players who missed 8 or more days after the initial
concussion, though this trend was not significant.

                                                              of
       Few studies have evaluated the risk of same-year repeat concussion at any level, and only
two studies at the NFL level exist. From 1996-2001, Pellman et al.16 reported that of 650 players
                                                        ro
who sustained a concussion, 36 (5.5%) sustained at least one same-season repeat concussion,
                                                  -p
which is similar to the 7.0% reported in this study. One explanation for the small difference is

                                            re
the inclusion of the off-season in our study, which accounted for two of the initial concussions in
the same-year concussion group. Unfortunately, Pellman et al. did not report the risk of same-
                                    lP
season repeat concussion for all NFL players in that time period, which in the current study was

                            na
low at 0.51%.16 Casson, et al.11 compared the data from the 1996-2001 and 2001-2006 seasons
and found that the risk of repeat concussions – more than one concussion in the study window
                      ur
and not same-season repeat concussion – remained similar across the two time periods (24.7%

               Jo
vs. 24.2%, respectively). While that study did not specifically report same-season repeat
concussions, it did note that the majority of players (89.8%) had more than 28 days between
concussions (average 456 days), with only 2.8% experiencing a repeat concussion within the
same week.11
       Since the publication of these early studies, and prior to the initial years of the current
study, several policy changes have been implemented regarding the management of concussed
players in the NFL, including indicators for immediate removal from play, a stepwise RTP
protocol, and mandatory evaluation by an independent neurological consultant.14 In the current
study, no player sustained a repeat concussion within 13 days of onset of the initial concussion.
Mack, et al., found that the concussion risk declined significantly in the 2018-2019 seasons
(6.2% and 7.1%, respectively) compared to the 2015-2017 seasons (7.4%-8.3%), thought to be
attributed to a dedicated focus on concussion awareness prior to the 2018 season.15 Additional



                                                                                                     6
                                                                                                Cools


rule changes after 2018 included elimination of blind-side blocks and updated kickoff rules.
Helmets were also tested in the laboratory,18 the results of which were made available to players
and teams. A subsequent policy mandated that players choose among higher performing helmets,
with poorer performing helmets being banned. Our data on same-year repeat concussions in the
same time interval do not demonstrate a significant decrease in the rate of same-year repeat
concussions, though 2019 did have the lowest rate (0.38%). This is likely due to the relatively
low numbers of same-year repeat concussions and a decrease in the denominator of overall
concussions.
        Same-year repeat concussions at the collegiate level also warrant discussion in the

                                                             of
context of elite American football. The National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA)
Concussion study (1999-2001) by Guskiewicz, et al.1 found a 6.5% risk of same-season repeat
                                                       ro
concussion among football players. In these athletes, the median RTP was 3.0 days and 91% of
                                                 -p
repeat concussions occurred within 10 days of the initial concussion. A subsequent study

                                           re
involving the Concussion Assessment, Research, and Education (CARE) Consortium, collecting
data from 2014-2017,6 found a same-season repeat concussion rate of 3.9%, demonstrating a
                                    lP
significant decline from the initial NCAA Concussion Study. RTP time was longer in the CARE

                            na
Consortium compared to the 1999-2001 study (median 12.2 days) and only 3.7% of same-season
repeat concussions occurred within 10 days of the initial concussion.6 Though comparisons
                      ur
between playing levels are made cautiously, the current NFL data demonstrate a higher risk of

                Jo
same-year season repeat concussion (6.8%) in NFL players compared to the CARE consortium
cohort of collegiate football players (3.9%).6,19 One explanation for higher risk of same-year
repeat concussion may be differences in the length of the study period. The current study
included the full NFL year (offseason, 4 preseason games, 16 regular season games, and
potential for 4 postseason games), which is longer than a NCAA season. The NCAA football
season typically runs from the beginning of workouts in July through late December or early
January bowl games, with between 12 and 1 games for most teams. Other explanations may
include differences in the style of play, access and availability of medical care, motivations for
RTP, differences in data collection, or other differences between collegiate and professional
football settings.
        The current study suggests that the risk of sustaining a same-year repeat concussion is
similar to the risk of sustaining a single concussion. Stable rates of same-year repeat and single



                                                                                                     7
                                                                                                 Cools


concussion are aligned with the likelihood that players have fully recovered by the time they
return from their injuries and re-enter the population at risk with a similar risk of sustaining a
concussion, rather than having an elevated risk for a repeat concussion. Hypothetically, if an
elevated risk of same-year repeat concussion compared to single concussions were to be found,
this may indicate a potential premature RTP following the initial concussion. Premature RTP has
been associated with a risk of additional concussion and a prolonged recovery,1 in addition to an
increased risk of musculoskeletal injury,20–22 or even second impact syndrome.23,24
       RTP times in our cohort were longer with repeat concussions (median 12 days) compared
to single concussions (median 9 days), which is also consistent with several previous studies

                                                              of
demonstrating prolonged recovery time from repeat concussions in high-school,25,26 collegiate,1,6
and professional27 sports. Though the current study cannot assess causation, these data may
                                                        ro
indicate that a second concussion within the same season may result in an injury requiring more
                                                  -p
recovery time. An alternative possibility is that team physicians and athletic trainers tend to be

                                            re
more cautious when athletes incur a second concussion in the same season. Both possibilities
require further empirical study.
                                    lP
       Among players with at least one concussion in a season, those who returned to play after

                             na
eight or more days were more likely to sustain a same-year repeat concussion than those who
returned to play after seven or fewer days, though this trend was not significant.26,27 The data
                       ur
suggest that a concussion resulting in longer RTP , likely representing a more severe concussion,

               Jo
may place players at higher risk for sustaining a same-year repeat concussion; players with 8 or
more days missed after an initial concussion had an estimated 48% higher risk of a same-year
repeat concussions than players with 7 or fewer days missed. Identifying additional risk factors
for repeat concussion may be able to help reduce the rate of repeat concussions.
       This study has limitations. This study focused on two or more concussions within an NFL
season; it did not evaluate concussions across multiple seasons or incorporate head injuries prior
to joining the NFL. It is possible that players had sustained one or more concussions prior to the
2015 season in or outside of the NFL, or sustained concussions across multiple seasons within
the study. Additionally, same-year repeat concussions may have been impacted by the timing of
the initial concussion within the season. For example, if a player sustained a concussion in the
latter portion of the year, they would have less time to sustain a same-year repeat concussion, as
there would be fewer opportunities to do so with the time remaining in the season. Conversely, a



                                                                                                     8
                                                                                                 Cools


player who sustained a concussion at the beginning of the year may have more opportunities to
sustain a same-year repeat concussion. Similarly, time to return to participation may have been
influenced by timing in the season and other factors. Notably, this analysis does not account for
granular time at risk for injury (e.g. player-games or player-days) as participation data outside of
games in limited. Also, our data do not account for limitations (e.g. play count or rep maximum)
placed on players by coaches, trainers, or athletes themselves once they are cleared for full
participation. However, investigating each NFL year as a unique interval allows for the study of
same-year risk for repeat concussion, which has not been reported since the newest iteration of
the NFL concussion protocols. The small number of same-year repeat concussions limits the

                                                              of
ability to perform subgroup analyses for timing of concussions during the year, though this may
be a topic for future study. This study benefits from the inclusion of all players within a single
                                                        ro
league, and consistency of data collection and robust, uniform detection procedures12,13,28 across
several seasons to minimize bias.                 -p
Conclusions
                                            re
                                    lP
       This study investigates the risk of same-year repeat concussion in the NFL over 5 seasons

                            na
from 2015 through 2019. Repeat concussions occurred at a similar rate to initial concussions,
indicating that players may not be at increased risk for a subsequent concussion when following
                      ur
evidence-informed RTP protocols. More missed time from an initial concussion was associated

               Jo
with an increased risk of repeat concussion, suggesting that a more severe concussion may be
associated with an increased risk of subsequent concussion. This study highlights the
effectiveness of a robust concussion identification system and RTP protocol. Physicians involved
in the evaluation and management of concussion should continue to pay significant attention to
the systems of identification of concussion, as well as their RTP protocols. Future research
should address risk factors for sustaining repeat concussions in order to enhance player safety.

4	                                                     A systematic review
5	                                                     Bryndan Lindsey1☯, Yosef Shaul2☯, Joel Martin            *

20	                                                     Abstract
21	                                                     Tactical athletes must maintain high levels of physical and cognitive readiness to handle
22	                                                     the rigorous demands of their roles. They frequently encounter acute stressors like sleep
23	                                                     deprivation, muscle fatigue, dehydration, and harsh environmental conditions, which
24	                                                     can impair their readiness and increase the risk of mission failure. Given the challenging
25	                                                     conditions these athletes face, there is a vital need for non-invasive, rapidly deployable
26	   OPEN ACCESS
27	                                                     point-of-care assessments to effectively measure the impact of these stressors on their
28	Citation: Lindsey B, Shaul Y, Martin J               operational readiness. Salivary biomarkers are promising in this regard, as they reflect

30	readiness: A systematic review. PLoS One             physiological changes due to stress. This systematic review aims to investigate salivary
31	20(4): e0321223. https://doi.org/10.1371/            markers as potential indicators for readiness, specifically focusing on their sensitivity
32	journal.pone.0321223

34	Editor: Juan Luis Castillo-                          cle fatigue. A search was conducted using the Preferred Reporting Items for System-
35	Navarrete, Universidad de Concepción Facultad
36	de Medicina: Universidad de Concepcion
37	                                                     atic Review and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines (PROSPERO; registration #:
38	Facultad de Medicina, CHILE                          CRD42022370388). The primary inclusion criteria were the use of a quantitative analysis
39	Received: August 14, 2024                            to assess salivary biomarkers changes in response to acute stressors. Risk of bias and

65	 and reproduction in any medium, provided the   Introduction
66	original author and source are credited.
67	                                               The occupational physiological demands of tactical athletes (TA), such as soldiers
68	Data availability statement: All relevant
69	                                               and emergency responders (police officers, fire fighters, emergency medical techni-
70	data are within the paper and its Supporting
71	Information files.                             cians, etc.) during stressful training and operational environments are comparable
72	                                               to that of competitive sporting athletes [1] and are often extreme, including extended
73	Funding: The author(s) received no specific
74	funding for this work.                         periods of high energy expenditure, dehydration, and limited sleep [2]. The subse-
75	                                               quent strain on physiology can cause fatigue [3] and degrade health and perfor-
76	Competing interests: The authors have
77	declared that no competing interests exist.    mance [4]. For the military and other tactical organizations, insufficient recovery and
78	                                               excessive training loads can increase the likelihood of injury [5] and may reduce
79	                                               operational readiness [5].
80	                                                  From a human performance perspective, operational readiness refers to the
81	                                               state of condition of individuals, which enables them to carry out their occupational
82	                                               duties effectively and efficiently [6]. Physical, cognitive, and emotional states can
83	                                               be altered rapidly due to the aforementioned stressors potentially impairing one’s
84	                                               level of operational readiness [6–8]. Traditional evaluation of TA operational read-
85	                                               iness includes medical examinations, fitness assessments, and subjective self-­
86	                                               assessment questionnaires, which can be imprecise, time-consuming, and often fail
87	                                               to predict performance outcomes [8]. Therefore, strategies to measure physiological
88	                                               readiness quickly and effectively in the field after exposure to occupational stressors
89	                                               are desired to objectively monitor TA status in-situ [9].
90	                                                  Stressors that impact operational readiness were outlined by a panel of military
91	                                               experts in 2013 and include physical fatigue, extreme environmental conditions
92	                                               (e.g., cold/hot temperatures, high altitude), altered psychological status (e.g., stress,
93	                                               anxiety, depression), and sleep quantity and quality [9]. When stressor events occur,
94	                                               sympathetic stimulation of the autonomic nervous system releases adrenaline and
95	                                               noradrenaline [10]. A secondary, slower response also occurs from stimulation of
96	                                               the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis which releases glucocorticoids such
97	                                               as cortisol [11]. Therefore, it has been hypothesized that measurement of such
98	                                               signaling molecules that induce physiological changes associated with acute stress
99	                                               may have diagnostic utility for TA operational readiness assessment [12]. Training
100	                                               induced changes in circulating levels of cortisol and testosterone show potential as
101	                                               markers of excessive training stress, physiological strain, and inadequate recov-
102	                                               ery in non-military populations [1,13]. These hormones have also been found to
103	                                               be sensitive to various forms of military training stress, with cortisol concentrations
104	                                               increasing during and following training [14,15] and total and free testosterone
105	                                               concentrations decreasing [16]. Additionally, other biomarkers have been associated
106	                                               with these stressors such as dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA) with physical stress
107	                                               [17], salivary pH with hypoxia from altitude [18], alpha amylase with sleep depriva-
108	                                               tion [19], and osmolality with dehydration [20], amongst others. Therefore, measure-
109	                                               ment of the biochemical signatures of stress shows promise to objectively quantify
110	                                               TA readiness and inform decision making in operational settings [7].
111	                                                  Biomarkers can be analyzed from various media including blood, urine, and/
112	                                               or saliva [7]. Serum-based biomarkers like cortisol [21], dehydroepiandrosterone
113	                                               (DHEA) [22], epinephrine and norepinephrine [23], neuropeptide-Y (NPY) [24],
114	
115	
116	
117	PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0321223 April 29, 2025                                                             2 / 27
118	 and brain derived neurotropic factor (BDNF) [25] have shown to be both responsive and potentially protective to military
119	related stressors like military training [21,23,25], while inflammatory cytokines like interleukin 6 (IL-6) [26], tumor necro-
120	sis factor (TNF-α) [26], and interleukin 10, (IL-10) [25] are well known to be responsive of exercise and training stress.
121	However, although blood has most often been used as the source of measurable biomarkers in diagnostic studies, there
122	are numerous advantages to the use of saliva, most notably including its ease of collection (e.g., non-invasive) and lower
123	risk of transmission [27]. In addition, saliva contains many analytes affected by a range of physiological and pathological
124	stressors [28,29] which have been highly correlated with those in blood [30,31], have shown good reproducibility and
125	changes across time [32], with research showing that analytes like salivary cortisol are associated with reduced perform-
126	ing after military training [33]. In fact, research has demonstrated strong positive correlations with serum levels for many
127	of the more commonly studied salivary biomarkers like cortisol (r = 0.92) [34], testosterone (r = 0.65) [35], and DHEA (r
128	= 0.86) [36]. Despite this, the use of saliva-based biomarkers as a diagnostic signal has yet to become widely adopted,
129	likely because although most analytes detected in blood are also found in saliva, their levels are diminished [37]. However,
130	due to the small quantities of fluid needed for extraction of biomarkers from saliva, the utility of the media still warrants
131	investigation.
132	    At present it is necessary to characterize the body of literature which has reported on the change in salivary biomarkers
133	after a variety of acute stressors to guide future research. Therefore, this systematic review seeks to explore and identify
134	salivary markers as potential candidates for diagnosing state of readiness. The main aim was to identify salivary markers
135	sensitive to acute stressors of sleep deprivation, dehydration, environmental, and muscular fatigue. Secondary aims were
136	to: (i) to identify salivary markers that are sensitive to physical readiness and (ⅱ) to identify salivary markers that are sen-
137	sitive to cognitive readiness. The systematic review aims hold practical importance as they provide valuable insights into
138	the relationship between salivary biomarkers and domains of operational readiness following exposure to common acute
139	stressors. By characterizing the existing literature and identifying salivary markers sensitive to stressors and cognitive
140	readiness, this review can guide future research and contribute to the development of non-invasive diagnostic tools for
141	monitoring operational readiness, potentially leading to reduced risks in high-demand environments.
142	
143	Materials and methods
144	Review registration
145	The study search criteria, screening, selection, data extraction, and quality assessment were defined a priori and informed
146	by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines (PRISMA) [38]. The system-
147	atic review was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; registration #:
148	CRDXXXXXXXXXXX – BLINDED).
149	
150	Eligibility criteria
151	The following inclusion criteria were applied to the review: a) published within the past 30 years, b) English language only,
152	c) peer reviewed articles, d) full text availability, e) human subjects research, f) healthy adults aged 18–60 years, g) investi-
153	gated salivary biomarkers as determinants of outcomes of ‘readiness’ in domains that include athletic performance, aerobic
154	and strength performance, or performance of cognitive tasks, h) incorporated acute stressors that included sleep deprivation,
155	dehydration, environmental, or muscle fatiguing activities, and i) quantified a change in biomarker due to an acute stressor.
156	Studies investigating biomarkers of disease (Alzheimer’s, diabetes, Parkinson’s, dementia, cancer) were excluded.
157	
158	Information sources
159	In line with recommendations for comprehensive literature coverage and recall [38], four databases—PubMed, CINAHL,
160	SportDiscus, and Google Scholar —were searched for relevant publications [39]. Google Scholar was searched using
161	
162	
163	
164	PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0321223 April 29, 2025                                                      3 / 27
165	 the Publish or Perish software [40]. The searches were conducted between January and February 2024. Additionally, the
166	reference lists of the retrieved articles were reviewed to identify any further potentially relevant studies not captured by our
167	initial search strategy [41].
168	
169	
170	Search strategy and study selection
171	A preliminary examination of topic-related studies was conducted to identify key search terms and categories. A set of
172	keywords and phrases using Boolean logic were then used to search relevant databases and identify original research for
173	review. Where possible, filters such as years since publication and language, were applied to meet eligibility criteria. If a
174	filter did not exist, eligibility was determined manually through screening of title and abstract. The list of search terms and
175	filters used to search the selected databases are detailed in S1 Table.
176	    Due to search string length limitation, the following string was applied for Google Scholar: saliva AND marker AND (ath-
177	letic | fitness | strength | aerobic | cognitive | psych* | exercise) AND performance AND (sleep | injury | dehydration | “acute
178	stress*”) -elderly -Alzheimer -Parkinson -dementia -Insomnia -cancer -diabetes -patient -child. Filters included English lan-
179	guage and past 30 years. Following previously published recommendations, the top 500 citations were exported instead
180	of top 200 [42].
181	    Two authors (YS and BL) conducted separate reviews on the four electronic databases. Full search results were
182	exported to SciWheel reference and citations manager (SAGE Publications, London, UK). Duplicates were searched for
183	and removed on SciWheel. Initial screenings of the titles and abstracts were independently conducted by two authors (YS,
184	BL) to assess whether eligibility criteria were met. In cases of a disagreement, a third author (JM) was consulted. The full
185	list of articles retrieved is provided in S2 Table.
186	
187	Data extraction and synthesis
188	For all eligible studies, data were extracted and tabulated independently by two authors (YS, BL). Data was extracted
189	from all eligible studies into a spreadsheet based on the Cochrane Consumers and Communication Review Group’s data
190	extraction template [43]. Extracted information included i) author, ii) year, iii) country, iv) title, v) participants, vi) study design,
191	vii) study description, viii) salivary biomarkers and collection method, ix) salivary biomarker quantification method, x) acute
192	stressors, xi) paired readiness outcome measures, xii) quantified change in biomarker concentrations, and xiii) key find-
193	ings. Statistically significant changes in readiness outcomes due to acute stressors were noted. Study design was classified
194	based on guidance provided by the Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine [44] with the addition of the definition of ‘quasi-­
195	experimental’ for non-randomized intervention studies. Following the data extraction, a qualitative synthesis was performed
196	regarding salivary biomarkers by acute stressor. Per the aims of the review, all studies meeting the eligibility criteria were
197	synthesized qualitatively with counts of significant changes in biomarkers per stressor tabulated and reported in text.
198	
199	Risk of bias and quality assessment
200	The included studies were evaluated for risk of bias and quality using the Downs and Black 27-item checklist, which
201	assesses methodological quality for both randomized and non-randomized studies. The checklist includes ratings for the
202	following constructs: reporting, external validity, bias, confounding, and power [45]. Of the 27 items, 25 are scored on a
203	scale of 0–1 point, with “yes” indicating the criterion is met (1 point) and “no/unable to determine” indicating it is not (0
204	points). Item 5, which assesses the detailing of confounders, scores as follows: “yes” equates to 2 points, partially to 1
205	point, and no to 0 points. Item 27 assesses statistical power on a scale up to 5 points. For this review, it was modified to
206	score “yes” (1 point) if the study detailed sufficient power to detect a clinically important effect, and “no/unable to deter-
207	mine” (0 points) otherwise [45]. This modification has been used in previous reviews [46] to reduce potential bias from
208	ambiguous wording [47].
209	
210	
211	
212	PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0321223 April 29, 2025                                                               4 / 27
213	    A total score was computed as the sum of the 27 items on the Downs and Black Checklist, and a percentage was
214	calculated by dividing the total score by the total possible points. These percentage scores were then used to determine
215	the overall quality of the studies. In this review, Kennelly’s [48] proposed grading system was modified from the original
216	Downs and Black checklist, changing the total possible points from 32 to 28. Consistent with previous reviews [46], stud-
217	ies scoring below 46.9% were classified as having ‘poor’ methodological quality, those scoring 46.9–62.5% as having ‘fair’
218	methodological quality, and those scoring above 62.5% as having ‘good’ methodological quality.
219	
220	Results
221	Search results
222	The PRISMA search diagram (Fig 1) depicts the results of the literature search, screening, and selection process. In
223	total, there were 2,386 search results, of which 1,207 duplicates were removed, yielding 1,179 studies. Title and abstract
224	screening yielded 95 studies that were screened for full text. Finally, 47 of these met the eligibility criteria while 2 more
225	were added during a backward/forward search to yield the final 49 included studies.
226	
227	Methodological quality
228	Article scoring on the Downs and Black checklist is displayed in Table 1. Included articles ranged from ‘fair’ (n=22) to
229	‘good’ (n=27) quality ratings with an overall mean(±SD) score of 18.5±1.3. On average, articles scored well on reporting
230	(80%) and internal validity - bias (73%), but poorly on external validity (33%) and internal validity - confounding (57%).
231	Only 5 of 49 studies reported performing a power analysis to ensure adequate sample size to detect significant differ-
232	ences. Specifically, most studies scored poorly (less than 25% scoring ‘yes’) on items 8, 14, 15, 23, 24, and 27. Addition-
233	ally, studies also only performed fair (less than 70% scoring ‘yes’) on items 5, 21, and 22.
234	
235	Characteristics of included studies
236	    General Characteristics. Details and key findings extracted from the included studies are reported in Fig 2 and
237	S3 Table. A majority (67%) of the research was conducted in the USA, Australia, and the United Kingdom. Most (71%)
238	were published within the last 10 years and none were older than 20 years. The average sample size of the included
239	studies was 23 out of a total 1,118 participants across all studies with ages in included samples ranging from 18–52
240	years. A diverse range of participants were represented in the included articles (Fig 2A), with 9 studies involving military
241	participants [17,33,49–55], as well as a variety testing athletes of sports like rugby [56–60], soccer [61–65], running
242	[66–68], rock climbers [69,70], weight-lifting [71,72], and cycling [20,73–75] amongst other sports [76,77]. Many also
243	simply tested healthy adults [1,18,19,78–85]. In addition, 2 studies considered emergency physicians and investigated the
244	exposure of health care personnel to acute stressors and possible implications on their performance and decision making
245	[86,87]. However, of the 49 studies, only 13 included both sexes, with a total of 194 males and 101 females in these
246	studies.
247	    Experimental methodology. Details on the designs, measured biomarkers, performance measures, and key findings
248	are reported in S3 Table. Twenty-two out of the 49 studies were prospective cohort studies in that they attempted
249	to describe how salivary markers change in response to stressors that are seen in a naturalistic setting but lacked
250	comparative control groups [17,33,49–51,53,54,57–60,64–66,68,70,77,86–90]. Twelve studies were quasi-experimental
251	in that the researchers measured response to imposed stressors pre-post [19,67,69,71,74,76,78,79,82,83,85,91]. Eleven
252	studies were randomized cross-over designs [18,20,56,61,63,72,73,80,81,84,75] while 3 randomized participants into
253	one of multiple stressor groups (parallel design) [52,55,62]. Only 1 study randomized participants into a stressor and
254	true control group [92]. Three of the studies reported a predictive model of a participant’s outcome based on levels of
255	salivary biomarkers [19,58,73]. Of these 3, a model was constructed to predict performance following fatigue [73] was
256

436	Biomarker Responses to Acute Stressors
437	    Muscle Damage and Physiological Fatigue. Twenty-six studies investigated salivary biomarker response to stressors
438	that can potentially cause muscle damage and fatigue such as military training, weight-lifting, rock climbing, ultra-endurance
439	events, and high intensity interval training [33,50,52,53,60,62–64,66,69–72,74,77,79–81,89,20,51,58,59,88,65,73].
440	The biomarkers studied in response to these stressors included cortisol [53,60,62–64,69,70,72,74,81,89,20,58,59,88],
441	testosterone [53,60,63,64,70,74,80,81,89,58,59,88], secretory immunoglobulin A (s-IgA) [50,64,66,74,20], alpha-amylase
442	[64,66,77,20], proteins and peptides [52,92,86,51], flow rate [66,20], metabolites [51], osmolality [52,20], creatine kinase
443	and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) [71], potassium and sodium [20], uric acid [65], total antioxidant capacity (TAC) [65],
444	thiobarbituric acid-reactive substances [65], mitochondrial DNA copy number (mtDNAcn) [79].
445	    Cortisol levels decreased in 6 studies [53,63,64,72,74,88], increased in 3 [62,69,70], and remained unchanged in 3
446	[20,59,81] as a response to induced muscle damage and/or physical fatigue. Other studies quantified cortisol levels as
447	predictors of performance with greater cortisol levels being associated with sporting performance [89] or win probability
448	[58]. Testosterone levels decreased in 3 studies [53,74,58], increased in 4 [63,80,88,59], and remained unchanged in 3
449	studies [64,70,81]. Like with cortisol levels, several studies investigated testosterone concentration as predictor of perfor-
450	mance and/or match outcome finding that both increases in testosterone levels after mid-week training exercises [58,59]
451	as well as lower testosterone on the morning of a match predictive of match success [88]. Several studies examined the
452	testosterone to cortisol ratio (T:C ratio) [61,64,65,71,75,82,20], with 4 reporting an increase [64,65,75,20], 1 reporting a
453	decrease [71], and 2 reporting no change [61,82].
454	    Changes in the expression of proteins and peptides after exercise, physically demanding training, and/or work-related
455	fatigue were explored in 4 studies with one study demonstrating reduced total salivary protein after 5 weeks of military
456	training compared to baseline [52]. Another 2 studies involved the identification of novel fatigue biomarkers from changes
457	in the abundance of peptides/proteins that predicted fatigue status at 83% [51] and 96% [86] accuracy while the last
458	developed a ‘fatigue biomarker index’ from a ratio of ion intensities from 2 novel peptides that was discriminatory of rating
459	of perceived exertion during an extended exercise trial [92]. In the same study that identified novel protein-based markers
460	of fatigue related to military training, a panel of small molecules (metabolites) were also identified yielding a discriminatory
461	value of 96% [51].

463	status of the athlete, decreasing if participants finished a 36-hour ultra-endurance event and increasing if they dropped out
464	or were stopped before 24 hours [66]. Alpha-amylase increased in 2 studies [77,20], remained unchanged in 1 [66], and

538	Discussion
539	The systematic review’s purpose was to identify salivary biomarkers sensitive to common stressors experienced by TA in
540	the existing literature. In regard to the first aim, multiple studies have identified salivary biomarkers that are responsive
541	to the acute stressors of muscle damage and physical fatigue, sleep deprivation, dehydration, and environmental stress
542	(see S3 Table). Hormonal biomarkers, such as testosterone and cortisol, were generally found to be sensitive to multiple
543	stressors; however, changes in protein expression and metabolite concentration appear to have greater utility to diag-
544	nose response to specific stressors. Our secondary aim was to quantify the impact of acute stressors on the response
545	of salivary biomarkers. However, the interpretation of reported results is challenging due to the heterogeneity of study
546	methodologies, making generalizable claims difficult. In most instances, changes in salivary biomarker levels were associ-
547	ated with reported physical or cognitive performance outcomes. This offers direction for future research aimed at exploring
548	non-­invasive approaches to assessing the state of readiness of TA in field settings.
549	
550	Salivary Biomarker Response to Acute Stressors
551	   Muscle Damage and Physiological Fatigue. The majority of studies examined the response of salivary biomarkers
552	to muscle damage and physiological fatigue, identifying creatine kinase, aspartate aminotransferase, uric acid, cortisol,
553	testosterone, and the T:C ratio as responsive markers. However, the direction of change (e.g., increase or decrease) and
554	magnitude of response of these markers varied widely across studies. For instance, cortisol and testosterone, two of the
555	most frequently measured biomarkers of muscle fatigue and damage, demonstrated mixed responses. Thus, the evidence
556	suggests that hormonal markers like cortisol and testosterone alone may lack the necessary sensitivity and specificity to
557	discriminate TA readiness to perform occupational duties due to their responsiveness to other factors like psychological
558	and social stress [96] and diurnal rhythm [97].
559	   Despite their individual limitations, there was evidence to support their combined utility. One study found that mid-
560	week levels of cortisol and testosterone predicted rugby match success with 72.2% accuracy [58]. Another study found a

566	losing games [59], suggesting that the T:C ratio may serve as a more reliable indicator of anabolic/catabolic balance which
567	is reflective of body strain (low ratio) or recovery (high ratio) [98]. Similarly, the ratio of DHEA-s, an anabolic HPA regulator,
568	to cortisol was explored in response to acute hypobaric hypoxia [55]. Despite the rapid increase in cortisol in response to
569	hypoxia, the overall DHEA-s to cortisol ratio remained the same [55], highlighting the potential utility of ratios over single
570	biomarkers for assessing stress resilience.
571	    Other biomarkers frequently studied included IgA [64,66,74,20] and alpha-amylase [64,66,77,91,20], which also exhib-
572	ited inconsistent directional results across studies. For example, Cook et al. reported decreased IgA levels in ultramara-
573	thon finishers, while non-finishers participating for more than 12 hours showed increased levels [56]. Additional salivary
574	biomarkers like creatine kinase [71], thiobarbituric acid-reactive substances (TBARS) [65] and uric acid [71,65] demon-
575	strated potential utility, albeit with varying response timelines. TBARS, a byproduct of oxidative stress, showed signifi-
576	cant increases post-professional soccer games before returning to baseline 48-hours after [65]. In comparison, creatine
577	kinase and uric acid exhibited delayed responses, with significant changes noted 48 [65] and 96 hours [71] post-exercise,
578	respectively. Uric acid in particular is known as a key salivary antioxidant and has shown to reliably indicate stress during
579	physical exertion as prior evidence has demonstrated that resistance training significantly elevates salivary uric acid levels
580	that were well correlated with serum markers of oxidate stress [99].
581	    Innovative approaches involving proteomics and metabolomics have identified promising markers for fatigue detection.
582	For instance, a panel of five proteins (e.g., periplakin, heat shock protein alpha family B member 9, myeloperoxidase,
583	heat shock protein family A member 9, and transketolase) discriminated between fatigued and non-fatigued individuals
584	with 83% accuracy following military training, while a panel of 5 metabolites (e.g., C16H13-ClN2O, gamma-butyrobetaine,
585	L-proline, proline-glycine, and pipecolic acid) achieved 96% accuracy in discriminating fatigue status in the same sample
586	[51]. The identified molecules associated with innate immunity, protein cycling and processing, and metabolism of sugars
587	and amino acids, were identified using a discovery approach in which samples were analyzed using mass spectrometry to
588	quantify all detectable proteins and/or metabolites. From which a subset that best predicted fatigue status was identified
589	using statistical techniques like linear discriminant analysis (LDA) [51] and Fisher discriminant analysis [86]. Other recent
590	evidence supports the use of the proteome to evaluate physical stress as proteins linked to immune response, antioxidant
591	activity, and structural integrity were found to be responsive to both exercise and sex [100]. Although not yet practical for
592	field settings, use of multi-omic analyses and machine learning techniques may allow for the discovery of novel combina-
593	tions of biomarkers that are more robust to some of the common confounders to predictions based off singular analytes
594	like diurnal rhythm or race (e.g., genetics), which can then be used to develop a novel assay.
595	    The greater responsiveness to fatigue of the markers found in these studies may be due to a variety of reasons includ-
596	ing their greater antigenicity [86], reduced susceptibility to non-exercise factors such as dietary and health conditions, and
597	perhaps most importantly, the availability of numerous proteins or metabolites involved in a wide variety of physiological
598	pathways. However, these discovered proteomic markers have not been studied as extensively as testosterone and
599	cortisol. Further research is necessary to characterize their responses to physical stress and establish their reliability for
600	operational readiness assessments.
601	    Sleep Deprivation. Cortisol levels consistently increased in response to sleep deprivation [57], with a noteworthy
602	decrease in the magnitude of the awakening response (e.g., the rapid cortisol rise 30 minutes after awakening) [78].
603	These findings align with previous evidence suggesting that sleep deprivation can impair HPA function. This impairment
604	results in elevated evening cortisol levels due to disruptions in glucocorticoid feedback mechanisms [101] and reduced
605	morning, cortisol secretion, reflecting alterations in normal circadian rhythm [102].
606	    In comparison to cortisol, the impact of sleep deprivation on testosterone levels was more variable. While testoster-
607	one tended to decrease following sleep deprivation [33,49,94], several studies reported no significant change [56,61].
608	This inconsistency may be due to methodological differences in factors like population studied, chronic vs acute
609	
610	
611	
612	PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0321223 April 29, 2025                                                      13 / 27
613	 sleep-deprivation, lack of standardization in sleep loss protocol, and/or different saliva collection time points. Evidence
614	suggests that the degree of sleep-deprivation is a critical factor where total sleep deprivation appears to reduce serum tes-
615	tosterone levels, while partial sleep-deprivation does not [103]. These trends were mirrored in the reviewed studies exam-
616	ining salivary testosterone as those with more intense sleep deprivation (e.g., from military training) [17,33,49] resulted in
617	decrease testosterone while those with less intense sleep loss did not [56,61]. The precursor to testosterone and other
618	steroid hormones, DHEA-s, also decreased following sleep deprivation from military training [17]. Additionally, decreased
619	levels of alpha-amylase were found in one study after extensive sleep-deprivation and was suggested to be sensitive to the
620	diurnal rhythm for arousal and capable of monitoring performance by closely tracking the diurnal drive for alertness [19].
621	    Proteomics-based studies further highlight the potential of advanced biomarker panels in assessing fatigue related
622	to sleep deprivation. Two studies investigating the impact of sleep deprivation on salivary biomarkers used proteomic
623	markers to predict fatigue status with one identifying clusters of peptides that successfully distinguished between fatigued
624	and non-fatigued groups with over 90% accuracy [92] and another identifying a group of 30 proteins and established a
625	model with 96% accuracy rate in discriminating between subjects fatigued from long-duration shift-work compared to non-­
626	fatigued subjects [86]. These findings highlight the potential for proteomics to enhance the precision of fatigue detection
627	caused by sleep deprivation. Panels of proteomic biomarkers may provide a more comprehensive and reliable method to
628	assess sleep quality and/or response to poor sleep, particularly in operational and occupational settings.
629	    Dehydration. Research has consistently demonstrated dehydration’s detrimental effects on various fitness
630	components, including aerobic performance [104–106], strength [107,108], power [109,110], and balance [111,112].
631	Additionally, reviews have found that a >2% BW loss impairs cognitive functions related to attention, executive function,
632	and motor coordination [113–115]. This body of evidence supports the need for hydration monitoring to maintain
633	operational readiness in the environments where TAs operate. As TAs frequently operate in environments where both
634	physical exertion and heat exposure are high, early detection and management of hydration status are essential for
635	maintaining both performance and operational effectiveness.
636	    Identification of hydration status using salivary biomarkers showed promised based on the results of the studies
637	included. Salivary properties such as increased osmolality and total protein concentration, and decreased flow rate
638	consistently indicated dehydration, particularly at moderate to severe levels [52,20,83,95]. These relationships are well-­
639	supported by physiological mechanisms, as dehydration alters salivary gland function through changes in serum osmolal-
640	ity and volume [116,117]. Additionally, dehydration triggers the release of acute phase proteins and an elevation in globulin
641	concentration [118]. Other biomarkers, such as cortisol and Cl-, also responded to dehydration [91]. Notably, Cl- was
642	particularly effective in detecting mild dehydration (~1.5% decrease of body weight), likely from to its stronger connection
643	to water movement due to its ionic nature This sensitivity suggests Cl- could enable early intervention before more severe
644	dehydration-related effects occur [91]. These findings are especially relevant as hydration is a critical concern for TAs
645	[119], with physical performance declining at dehydration levels of >2% body weight, particularly under heat stress [120].
646	    Environmental Stress. The primary environmental stressors addressed in the studies included were temperature
647	and altitude. Altitude-induced stress was associated with elevated levels of cortisol [67,90,55], DHEA-s [55], and salivary
648	pH [18]. Cortisol and DHEA-s levels increase with elevated altitude as a physiological adaptation to the reduced oxygen
649	availability at higher altitudes, prompting adaptation of the HPA axis [121,122]. Salivary pH may also rise due to changes
650	in buffering capacity influenced by hypoxia [123]. While altitude exposure may be less relevant for monitoring the
651	readiness of TAs compared to more common acute stressors like sleep deprivation, dehydration, and muscle fatigue/
652	damage, the physiological effects of high altitude are well documented [124] and can still pose challenges to operational
653	readiness in specific contexts. In addition, the effect of cold temperature was investigated in a single study whereby
654	exercise in cold temperatures relative to normal temperatures resulted in decreased osmolality but not salivary IgA [75].
655	Although limited, this finding suggests that cold environments may influence certain salivary biomarkers differently than
656	other stressors, warranting further exploration to understand the implications for TA readiness in extreme conditions.
657	
658	
659	
660	PLOS One | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0321223 April 29, 2025                                                  14 / 27
661	    Multi-Stressor. Several studies incorporated multiple stressors, predominantly within military populations
662	[33,52–54,51], enhancing ecological validity by more accurately reflecting the multifaceted nature of military duties
663	better than studies with single stressors. These findings offer a more comprehensive understanding of the physiological
664	responses to complex, real-world stressors. Notably, inconsistent cortisol responses observed in these studies [33,53,54],
665	highlight the variability of stress reactions in different individuals and situations. The decreases in testosterone levels and
666	the T:C ratio following military training suggest a potential overtraining effects [125–127], which is critical for developing
667	effective training and recovery protocols. Conversely, the increase in DHEA-s levels increased during stressful captivity
668	training, along with the variations in DHEA-s to cortisol ratio between morning and evening, indicates an adaptive
669	response to prolonged stress [54].
670	   Signs of dehydration during military training, evidenced by increased osmolality and decreased protein concentration
671	[52], emphasize the need for proper hydration strategies to maintain TA operational readiness. Lastly, while most studies
672	focused on standard hormonal panels and salivary properties, one study’s use of proteomic and metabolomic profiling to
673	identify proteins linked to chronic stress and distinguish acute battle-related stress events underscores the potential for
674	advanced biomarker analysis in understanding stress responses [51].
675	   The collective findings from the studies reviewed have identified several salivary biomarkers, as depicted in Fig 3,
676	which show promise for detecting exposure to specific acute stressors frequently encountered by TA. These salivary bio-
677	markers appear to mirror either a systemic reaction to acute stressors or responses specific to certain conditions. Cortisol,
678	a key marker of HPA axis activation, indicates physiological stress across various types of stressors, and affects nearly
679	every tissue due to the widespread presence of cortisol receptors [10]. Cortisol also influences the levels of other signif-
680	icant biomolecules, such as alpha amylase [128], demonstrating its broad physiological impact. However, while cortisol
681	serves as a general indicator of stress, it may lack the specificity needed to differentiate between individual responses or
682	distinct stressors. Additionally, testosterone levels and the T:C ratio offer additional insights to the anabolic-to-
683	catabolic balance, which is crucial for muscle recovery and adaptation [129]. While cortisol and testosterone reflect
684	systemic responses and deliver valuable information, proteomic analyses provide further insight into cellular processes,
685	revealing more distinct biological markers [130]. This finer resolution aids in understanding the unique signatures associ-
686	ated with different physiological stressors and may guide the development of targeted strategies to monitor and mitigate
687	the effects of acute and chronic stressors in TAs.

                                               The occupational physiological demands of tactical athletes (TA), such as soldiers

                                               to that of competitive sporting athletes [1] and are often extreme, including extended
